data.hypothesis: The selected lead-directed decoder was valid but measured slower than baseline, while predicate aggregation was valid and near baseline speed; neither result establishes the cause. This pure-scalar variant tests whether deriving the continuation count from lead comparisons and sharing a continuation loop reduces the width-specific control flow. The extra loop and boundary checks may instead cost more, so controller measurement is needed.

memory_lessons.applicability: Branch-reduced scalar UTF-8 experiments on this workload; results do not identify a cause for the measured timing differences.
memory_lessons.claim: The lead-directed candidate measured 56.50 µs versus the baseline's 49.62 µs, while the predicate-aggregation candidate measured 49.55 µs. These measurements do not establish why either variant performed as it did.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the shared-loop candidate against the same official workload and correctness cases; avoid attributing performance to branch reduction without supporting measurements.

memory_lessons.applicability: When revisiting compact DFA UTF-8 decoding.
memory_lessons.claim: A compact-DFA development record failed protected correctness checks; the available evidence does not identify the cause.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Audit transition handling against malformed and boundary UTF-8 cases before measuring another compact DFA.

data.notes: Pure-scalar candidate; no performance claim is made before controller measurement. A prior compact-DFA development variant (e87168de8c614fc4-h01) failed protected correctness checks; the available record does not identify why. This proposal uses a shared continuation loop instead of reusing that DFA.
transformations: Retain the ASCII-run fast path and the existing ABI and output behavior.
Replace separate width-specific continuation validation with a continuation count derived from lead-byte comparisons and a shared loop.
Check the remaining length before continuation loads and preserve the E0, ED, F0, and F4 second-byte restrictions.
